title: A bar in Minnesota, three owners and a bucket of green onions
lede: Two stories are told about Chi-Chi’s. In one, a hepatitis outbreak destroyed a healthy chain. In the other, which is the one in the filings, a chain that had been shrinking for a decade ran out of money first and then ran out of luck.

chapters.title: Half of a football player’s bar
chapters.cap: first-year sales, against a forecast of $400,000
chapters.body:
The first Chi-Chi’s opened in half of the Left Guard, a bar and restaurant in Richfield, Minnesota owned by Max McGee, a former Green Bay Packers receiver.[^1][^42] The idea was Marno McDermott’s. He had already built a Mexican fast-food business, Zapata Foods, and sold it to Heublein for $4M, and he believed Minnesotans would pay for a sit-down version.[^1] The company’s own history said the name was his wife’s nickname.[^1]

Sources do not agree on the year. A reference history and the revived company say 1975; the chain’s own website in 1998 said 1976.[^1][^2][^38] They agree on what happened next. The first-year forecast was $400,000 and sales reached $2M.[^1][^2]

A Minneapolis stockbroker, John Stephens, bought the rights to operate and franchise the restaurants. In October 1977 Shelly Frank, a 33-year-old vice president at Kentucky Fried Chicken, became president, and the headquarters moved to his home town of Louisville.[^1] In five years the system went from four restaurants to 92 and revenue from slightly more than $1M to $97.6M.[^1] A former executive later summed up the offer: “It took Mexican food and really put in full-service quality with fast-food pricing.”[^15]

A reference history says 42 restaurants opened in 1985 alone, that net income peaked in 1984 at $16.7M and that the chain had 200 restaurants by 1986. It also describes what the pace cost: restaurants of 10,000 to 12,000 square feet that were too large to run profitably, failed entries into New York and New England, and management turnover as high as 80% in company-owned restaurants.[^2]

pull.text: You got a lot of food for a reasonable price. And there were the margaritas.
pull.who: Jack Butorac, former Chi-Chi’s vice president, The Courier-Journal, Nov 30, 2003[^15]

image.caption: The “Chi-Chi’s History” page of chi-chis.com as the Internet Archive captured it on May 9, 1998. It dates the first restaurant to 1976.[^1]
image.alt: A plain web page headed Chi-Chi’s History with paragraphs of text under the subheadings Roots and Building the Team

chapters.title: Sold to the owners of Jack in the Box
chapters.cap: paid by Foodmaker in April 1988, as reported later
chapters.body:
Frank retired in 1986 and Hal Smith, who had run Chili’s, took over. By a reference history’s account he cut corporate staff by 18%, shortened managers’ hours, brought management turnover down to 35% within a year and closed 21 marginal restaurants, taking a $20M write-off.[^2]

In April 1988 Foodmaker Inc. of San Diego, the owner of Jack in the Box, bought the company. The price is given as about $235M for 129 company-operated restaurants, with 77 more franchised.[^1][^2][^15] The same history calls 1990 the chain’s best year, with sales of $450M, and says that by 1992 guest counts were falling at its 160 company-owned and 65 franchised restaurants while Taco Bell and casual-dining chains took customers.[^2] Foodmaker’s own accounts show Chi-Chi’s sales of $404.5M in the fiscal year that ended on October 3, 1993.[^11]

Not everyone blamed the market. Jack Butorac, who left Chi-Chi’s two years before the sale, told Louisville’s Courier-Journal in 2003 that Foodmaker “tried to convert it to a California concept,” and that the company had borrowed against Chi-Chi’s real estate to pay for the purchase.[^15] That is one former executive’s view; we have no filing that tests it.

In 1992 Chi-Chi’s bought a major franchisee, Consul Restaurant Corp., out of Chapter 11 for $8.7M in cash and kept 22 of its 26 restaurants.[^2][^11]

pull.text: They tried to convert it to a California concept.
pull.who: Jack Butorac, on Foodmaker, The Courier-Journal, Nov 30, 2003[^15]

chapters.title: A write-off in the first year
chapters.cap: fall in sales at comparable Chi-Chi’s restaurants in 1996
chapters.body:
On January 27, 1994 Foodmaker, Apollo and Green Equity Investors took control of Restaurant Enterprises Group, which had been through a bankruptcy reorganization, renamed it Family Restaurants Inc. and merged Chi-Chi’s into it.[^2][^11] The filing put the price of Chi-Chi’s at about $270.0M including assumed debt, for a business that operated or franchised 235 restaurants. The new company sold $300.0M of senior notes and $150.0M of discount notes and opened a $150.0M credit line.[^3][^46]

Before the year was out it wrote off all $144.78M of the goodwill recorded for Chi-Chi’s.[^3]

From 1996 the filings report the division on its own, and the numbers run one way. Company-operated restaurants went from 184 at the end of 1996 to 128 at the end of 2002. Sales went from $278.1M to $186.4M, a fall of 33% (derived). Sales at comparable restaurants dropped 11.5% in 1996 and 8.2% in 1997, rose 1.8% in 1998, then fell every year after.[^4][^5][^6][^7] In late 1998 the company marked 48 Chi-Chi’s for sale or closure and set aside $22.9M for it.[^5]

The parent kept changing shape around it. It sold its family-restaurant division in 1996, bought Koo Koo Roo and Hamburger Hamlet in October 1998, renamed itself Prandium in 1999 and sold El Torito in June 2000, which left Chi-Chi’s as its largest business.[^2][^4][^6] On May 6, 2002 Prandium filed a pre-packaged Chapter 11 of its own. The plan took effect on July 2. Nine months later its annual report said the results raised “substantial doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern.”[^7]

pull.text: These matters raise substantial doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern.
pull.who: Prandium Inc., annual report for 2002, filed Mar 31, 2003[^7]

chapters.artCaption: Original illustration of a closed restaurant with a blank sign. Not a drawing of a real location.

chapters.title: Bankruptcy first, then the outbreak
chapters.cap: patients in the CDC’s final count; three died
chapters.body:
A plan to sell all of Prandium for $6.4M in cash fell apart in the summer of 2003 when one of the investors pulled out.[^8][^17] On October 8, 2003 Chi-Chi’s, Inc. and Koo Koo Roo filed for Chapter 11 in Delaware. Chi-Chi’s listed debts of more than $100M and said it ran 128 restaurants in 20 states. It had a non-binding letter of intent from a buyer, a company controlled by the entertainment promoter Jack Utsick.[^9][^15][^16]

That same week, people who ate at the Chi-Chi’s in the Beaver Valley Mall in Monaca, Pennsylvania were being infected with hepatitis A. Of the patients who could recall a single visit, 84% had eaten there between October 3 and October 6.[^13] Nobody knew until emergency-room doctors noticed the cases. The state health department issued an advisory on November 3 and the restaurant closed.[^25]

The CDC found the source in the mild salsa, which was made in batches of 40 to 80 quarts with raw green onions and served free with chips to every table. The onions had been grown in Mexico and were contaminated before they reached the restaurant. They were stored for up to five days in a shared bucket with the ice they were shipped in, which the investigators said let clean and contaminated bundles mix.[^12][^13] No restaurant worker was the source.[^13]

The CDC’s final count was 601 patients, at least 124 of them hospitalized, and three deaths. About 9,000 people were given immune globulin.[^12][^13] The Associated Press called it the biggest known outbreak of hepatitis A in U.S. history.[^14] The chain pulled green onions from every restaurant. Its sale did not happen.[^14][^15]

pull.text: There’s no definitive information that green onions played a role. However, we don’t know. Authorities are looking at them.
pull.who: Bill Zavertnik, chief operating officer of Chi-Chi’s, Associated Press, Nov 15, 2003[^14]

chapters.artCaption: Original illustration of green onions stored root side down in a bucket of ice, as the CDC described the restaurant’s practice.[^12] Not a photograph.

chapters.title: Outback buys the buildings
chapters.cap: restaurant properties whose rights went to Outback Steakhouse
chapters.body:
Chi-Chi’s spent 2004 in Chapter 11 settling claims from the outbreak through its insurers. By September about 150 of some 325 claims had been settled for $7M.[^20]

On August 3, 2004 the bankruptcy court approved Outback Steakhouse as the winning bidder for the “designation rights” to 76 properties: the power to take each site for itself, pass it to someone else or hand it back. Outback paid $42.5M.[^18] It wanted the sites for its own restaurants. Its senior vice president told the Associated Press that the deal did not include the Chi-Chi’s brand, its restaurant operations or any recipes.[^20]

The sale closed on September 20, 2004, and the restaurants stopped trading.[^19][^21] The chain’s website was replaced with one sentence on a stucco-colored background.[^22] A recorded message on its guest-relations line said the chain was no longer in business.[^20]

By the end of the year Outback had assigned its rights to 25 of the properties to a third party for $9.975M, told Chi-Chi’s to keep 15, and still held 35.[^19]

pull.text: We would like to thank all of our loyal customers of the past 27 years and with a tear in our eye, say ¡Adios!

image.caption: The whole of chi-chis.com after the closing, from an Internet Archive capture of October 10, 2004.[^22]
image.alt: A textured orange web page with one line of text thanking customers of the past 27 years and saying Adios

chapters.title: A jar of salsa and one restaurant
chapters.cap: Chi-Chi’s restaurant open in the United States in October 2026
chapters.body:
The lawsuits outlasted the restaurants. By December 2005 the chain and its insurers had paid more than $40M, including $6.25M to a man who needed a liver transplant, and an $800,000 class settlement for people who had only needed shots: 4,931 of them received $162.23 each.[^23][^24]

The name never left the supermarket. Hormel Foods sells Chi-Chi’s salsa, chips and tortillas, and since 2009 the brand has sat in MegaMex Foods, Hormel’s joint venture with Mexico’s Herdez Del Fuerte.[^26][^28] Abroad, franchised restaurants carried on. A Belgian operator had fifteen in Belgium and two in Germany in 2014, and two in Luxembourg closed in September 2019 when their franchise agreement ended.[^39][^40]

In December 2024 Michael McDermott, Marno McDermott’s son, announced an agreement with Hormel, which owns the trademarks, to open restaurants under the name.[^29][^30] He raised money from the public through a crowdfunding campaign with a $250 minimum; it had brought in $2.4M shortly before the opening.[^32][^33] On October 6, 2025 a Chi-Chi’s opened at 1602 West End Boulevard in St. Louis Park, Minnesota, in the space of his Rojo Mexican Grill.[^35][^36] A second conversion, in Maple Grove, did not go ahead; that building was reported to be too small.[^37]

When we checked on October 8, 2026 the restaurant’s website listed that one location.[^38]

pull.text: Chi-Chi’s is coming back stronger than ever.
pull.who: Michael McDermott, press release quoted by Fox 9, Aug 19, 2025[^34]
